title: Climate change is literally altering the shape of our planet

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A university student and her professor discuss a research project on satellite data and its limitations.

script.en: Professor, I've been reading about how scientists use satellite data to measure changes in the Earth's surface. But I'm confused about why they still need ground-based stations if satellites can cover the whole planet.

That's a good question. Satellites do provide broad coverage, but their signals can be affected by the atmosphere, and they don't give you the same level of precision as a fixed station on the ground. Ground stations act as reference points to calibrate the satellite data.
So the ground stations are like anchors? But I read that there are very few stations near the poles or in the middle of the ocean. Doesn't that leave big gaps?

Exactly. And that's a major challenge. In remote oceans, you'd need to place stations on buoys, which is expensive and logistically difficult. Near the poles, the harsh conditions make maintenance hard. So we have to rely on models to fill in the gaps, and that introduces uncertainty.
I see. For my project, I want to compare different methods for tracking the Earth's shape changes. Would it be better to focus on the gravity field data or the GNSS measurements?

Actually, the most interesting research compares both. They don't always agree perfectly, and understanding why can reveal a lot about what's happening beneath the surface. For instance, the solid Earth might be rising in one place while the ocean water redistributes and causes a different effect.
So the discrepancies are not just errors—they're clues?
Precisely. That's the kind of critical thinking I hope to see in your project. Just make sure you don't treat the two datasets as interchangeable; each has its own strengths and limitations.

script.en: A new study was published in the Journal of Geophysical Research. It shows that the Earth's shape is slowly becoming rounder. The speed of this change is increasing, and this has surprised many researchers. The research was led by a team of geodesists, and they used data from the Global Navigation Satellite System. This let them track small movements of the Earth's crust over time with great precision. The findings show that between 2011 and 2015, the poles rose. At the same time, the equatorial bulge shrank by about one millimeter per year. This is a small but measurable change in the planet's overall shape. The Earth's diameter is nearly 13,000 kilometers, so this may seem unimportant. However, the rate is more than double what it was in the late 1990s. This means the process is speeding up, and the main cause of this change is the melting of polar ice caps. Melting ice reduces pressure on the crust, and this allows the crust to rise slowly over many decades. At the same time, water from the melting ice flows toward the equator. This increases mass there and further reduces the bulge, and in this way, the trend is strengthened. However, the picture becomes more complex when oceans are included. The redistribution of water actually makes the planet slightly flatter overall. This is because the ocean bulges at the equator. This effect is stronger than the rounding effect in the solid rock. The researchers also compared their GNSS measurements with gravity field data. They found that the two do not perfectly match. This suggests that the Earth's shape and its gravity field do not move in perfect step as previously thought. Still, using both methods together can give a fuller understanding of how climate change is reshaping the planet. This is especially true in sensitive regions like Greenland and Antarctica, and the study shows the importance of long-term monitoring. It also points to the need for better station coverage in remote areas to reduce uncertainty.

sections.title: Earth's Changing Shape: A Climate Signal
sections.passage: Our planet is not a perfect sphere, and its rotation makes it flat at the poles and wide at the equator. Scientists have known this for a long time, and but a recent study in JGR Solid Earth shows that Earth is becoming rounder faster than before. The main cause is the melting of polar ice caps, and this finding has caught much attention from scientists. The research was led by Christoforos Kotsakis, a professor of geodesy, and his team used direct measurements from the global navigation satellite system (GNSS). This system can track the planet's shape changes with great precision over time. However, GNSS has limits, and there are few stations near the poles and in remote oceans. Equipment there must be placed on buoys, and this makes full coverage hard to achieve. To solve this problem, Kotsakis developed a new method to better capture surface changes. He found that between 2011 and 2015, the poles rose and the equatorial bulge shrank by about one millimeter per year. This rate is more than double the 0.5 millimeters per year seen between 1997 and 2000. It shows an acceleration of about 0.4 millimeters per year each decade. This trend has important meaning for our understanding of how the planet works. The cause is polar ice melt, and melting ice reduces pressure on the Earth's crust. The crust then slowly rebounds, much like bread dough springing back after being pressed. At the same time, more mass moves toward the equator, and this puts pressure on the crust there and reduces its bulge. However, when we consider the solid Earth and the ocean together, the planet is actually getting flatter by about 0.8 millimeters per year. This is because the ocean bulges at the equator as water moves away from the poles. This "water weight" is stronger than the rounding in the rock below, and it creates a complex interplay between different parts of the Earth system. Researchers also track Earth's changing shape using gravity field measurements, and these measurements change with regional mass. Kotsakis found that GNSS changes and gravity field measurements do not match perfectly. This suggests that the planet's shape and gravity field are not in perfect step. But the two methods can be combined to track the major effects of climate change. These effects include the melting of Greenland and Antarctica and the changing movements of ocean water. Together they give a fuller picture of ongoing environmental changes, and the study stresses the importance of long-term monitoring. It also points to the need for better station coverage in remote areas to reduce uncertainties. As climate change continues to change how mass is distributed on Earth's surface, understanding these small shape changes will be key. It will help predict future sea-level rise and other environmental impacts, and this makes continued research in this field essential.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about GNSS and gravity data?

They provide complementary information about Earth's changes.
Gravity data is more reliable than GNSS measurements.
GNSS data should replace gravity field measurements.
questions.explain: 正确项由原文“两者不完美匹配但可结合追踪气候变化影响”推断为互补。A项“完全无关”过于绝对，与可结合矛盾；B项“更可靠”无依据，属过度推断；C项“取代”与原文结合使用相反。
questions.evidence: But the two methods can be combined to track the major effects of climate change.

rapid acceleration
complete separation

questions.evidence: This suggests that the planet's shape and gravity field are not in perfect step.

long_sentences.en: However, there's a catch: When considering the solid Earth and the ocean together, the planet is getting flatter by about 0.03 inches (0.8 mm) a year because the ocean is getting bulgier at the equator as water shifts away from the poles.

The shift is being driven by polar ice melt, which takes pressure off the Earth's crust and allows it to rise slowly, similar to how rising bread dough springs back after you press a finger into it, Kotsakis reported.

She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association.
